items.title: Common-garden metabolomics reveals germplasm-associated metabolic diversity and candidate resources for functional food development in dried jujube (Ziziphus jujuba Mill.)
items.authors: Shi-Yong Wen, Wen-Jia Leng, Hai-Yang Wang, Li-Guo Qiu, Wen-Jiao Li, Lan Wang
items.abstract: Dried jujube ( Ziziphus jujuba Mill.) is valued for its nutritional and medicinal properties. However, metabolic assessments of jujube germplasm based on materials collected from different geographical regions are often confounded by environmental variation, making it difficult to distinguish germplasm-associated metabolic differences from environmental effects. This study aimed to characterize metabolic diversity among dried jujube germplasm resources under common-garden conditions and identify candidate resources with favorable nutritional and functional metabolite profiles. A total of 66 dried jujube germplasm resources originating from diverse regions of China were cultivated under a common environment and evaluated using LC-MS/MS-based broad-targeted metabolomics. Metabolic profiles were characterized by principal component analysis, uniform manifold approximation and projection, and hierarchical clustering. The accumulation patterns of major nutritional and functional metabolite classes were further compared for comprehensive evaluation of germplasm resources. A total of 460 metabolites were annotated, mainly including organic acids, terpenoids, flavonoids, nucleotides and derivatives, and lipids. Multivariate analyses revealed distinct metabolic profiles among germplasm resources, whereas metabolic clustering did not fully correspond to geographical origin, indicating substantial germplasm-associated variation under common-garden conditions. Organic acids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, triterpenoids, and alkaloids showed relatively large variation among germplasm resources and contributed substantially to differences in metabolic and nutritional profiles. items.title: Leaf Phenotypic Variation in Natural Populations of Chestnuts in Yağlıdere Forests (Giresun, Türkiye)
items.authors: N. Pul, Saim Zeki Bostan
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate phenotypic diversity and population relationships among natural chestnut (Castanea sativa Mill.) populations in the forests of Yağlıdere district (Giresun, Türkiye) based on leaf morphological traits. Leaf samples were collected from 105 seed-propagated trees representing seven populations during the 2020 and 2021 growing seasons. Eleven leaf parameters, including lamina dimensions, petiole length, tooth characteristics, and leaf area, were measured, and several ratio-based traits were calculated. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, analysis of variance, principal component analysis (PCA), and hierarchical cluster analysis were applied to two-year average data. Significant differences were detected among genotypes and populations for most leaf traits. Strong correlations were observed among leaf size-related parameters, whereas marginal traits showed more variable relationships. PCA revealed that the first three components explained more than 80% of the total variation at the genotype level and over 90% at the population level, with leaf size, shape ratios, and tooth characteristics being the main contributors to morphological differentiation. Hierarchical clustering produced grouping patterns consistent with PCA results, clearly discriminating genotypes and populations based on leaf morphology. The findings demonstrate that leaf morphological traits provide a reliable and practical approach for the characterization, conservation, and utilization of chestnut genetic resources.

items.abstract: Although red dates (Ziziphus jujuba Mill.) are rich in nutrients and have both edible and medicinal properties, during the drying process, due to their high sugar content, they often result in a lower glass transition temperature (Tg), enhanced hygroscopicity, surface agglomeration, and a decline in storage quality, severely limiting the shelf stability of the products and the improvement of the processing quality. Cold plasma (CP) can form cavities through surface etching, promoting water migration, thereby increasing the drying rate and diffusion coefficient. Vacuum pulsation drying (PVD) has a higher drying rate, stronger mass transfer ability, and better quality retention effect compared to ordinary drying methods. Based on these characteristics, we believe that CP and PVD have a synergistic enhancing effect in the drying of date slices. Therefore, in this study, CK-PVD (without plasma pre-treatment, direct vacuum pulsation drying) was used as the control group, and CP-PVD (after plasma pre-treatment, vacuum pulsation drying), A1, A2, and A3 (after plasma treatment, soaking in different concentrations of ethanol and then vacuum pulsation drying) were used as experimental groups to study the effects of CP pre-treatment combined with ethanol extraction on the sugar composition, glass transition temperature (Tg), physical stability, and reduce blood sugar activity of dried date slices. The results showed that CP pre-treatment significantly improved the material transfer efficiency (confirmed by the increases in the areas of T22 and T23 peaks). items.title: Comparative Performance of Stearoyl Chloride-Modified Cellulose Sponges from Five Lignocellulosic Wastes for Oil/Water Separation
items.authors: Emrecan Arpaci, Sami Imamoğlu
items.abstract: Increasing industrial activity and oil spills have turned oil pollution into a serious threat to aquatic ecosystems. This study compares five lignocellulosic wastes—rice husk, chestnut shell, tissue dust, cotton lint and chemical pulp—as raw materials for chemically modified cellulose sponges as a sustainable oil-removal solution. Cellulose fibres were converted into three-dimensional porous sponges by freezing and lyophilisation, then rendered hydrophobic and oleophilic by esterification with stearoyl chloride, confirmed by a new ester carbonyl band in the FTIR spectra of all five sample series. After modification, static water contact angles increased from a superhydrophilic 0° to 115–136.5°, and the sponges adsorbed oils and organic solvents at 12–17 times their own dry weight, retaining over 70% of this capacity after ten regeneration cycles. Chemical purity (α-cellulose content and lignin/extractive ratio) was the main determinant of performance: sponges from cotton lint and chemical pulp outperformed those from unprocessed agricultural wastes (rice husk, chestnut shell) in hydrophobicity and sorption capacity, while the latter showed compensating gains in mechanical strength. These findings indicate that lignocellulosic-waste-derived cellulose sponges are an environmentally friendly, high-performance sorbent with strong potential for oil-spill clean-up and oily wastewater treatment, with raw material choice guided by the intended application’s priorities.

items.title: Metabolic convergence on TOR signaling in the chestnut blight fungus and its regulation by host plant signals.
items.authors: Yo-han Ko, Jeesun Chun, Geonmin Kim, Jiwon Yu, Dae-Hyuk Kim
items.abstract: Transcriptomic analysis of the chestnut blight fungus Cryphonectria parasitica identified 22 core genes regulated by Cryphonectria hypovirus 1 (CHV1) infection and sectorization. Twelve genes with common phenocopies were analyzed: all mutants displayed restricted colonial growth, intense pigmentation, hyperbranched terminal hyphae with swollen globose cells, and reduced conidiation. Although gene-specific mutant phenotypes existed, responses to most stressors were similar to those of the wild-type. Mutant growth was highly sensitive to nutrient conditions, and growth restriction was notably alleviated by supplementation with 1.0 M sorbitol, nutrient-deficient media, or skim milk. All mutants showed hallmarks consistent with reduced target of rapamycin (TOR) signaling. Trehalose accumulation, a canonical fungal response to TOR inhibition, was observed in mutants via transcriptional upregulation of core trehalose biosynthetic genes, resulting in altered hyphal osmolarity and common mutant cell phenotypes. Plant signals overrode the mutants' phenotypes, strongly promoting their growth and differentiation. Although a severely retarded growth defect was observed in mutants, mutants' virulence remained intact, which can be ascribed to the host-plant signals. Cryphonectria hypovirus 1 (CHV1)-infected mutants exhibited greater growth restriction, accompanied by genotype-specific CHV1 titers. Despite gene-specific variation, common phenocopies indicate that diverse metabolic pathways converge on the TOR pathway in the fungal response to host-plant and CHV1 infection.

items.title: Repeat-Rich Architecture and Gene Duplication Characterize the Expanded Genome of the Chestnut Gall Wasp
items.authors: Ye-Song Ren, An-Kang Lv, Yang Zeng, Dao-Hong Zhu
items.abstract: Dryocosmus kuriphilus, the chestnut gall wasp, is a globally invasive pest that reproduces by thelytokous parthenogenesis. Despite the absence of conventional sexual recombination, the species has spread widely and persists under diverse environmental conditions, but the genomic features associated with this capacity remain poorly understood. Here, a chromosome-level assembly of D. kuriphilus was compared with seven representative insect genomes, with emphasis on repetitive sequences, orthogroups, and gene-duplication patterns. The 2.28-Gb D. kuriphilus genome contained 79.7% repetitive sequences, including 62.3% transposable elements (TEs), most of which occurred in intergenic regions. OrthoFinder assigned 13,271 D. kuriphilus genes to multi-copy orthogroups, representing 61.5% of the protein-coding gene set. Independent MCScanX analysis classified genes into mutually exclusive dispersed, proximal, tandem, and segmental duplication modes, with segmental and dispersed representing the two largest duplicated-gene classes. D. kuriphilus contained substantially more segmental duplicates than the other species examined. Synonymous-substitution distributions revealed low- and high-Ks components representing different levels of synonymous divergence among duplicated genes, and genes in these components showed distinct functional profiles. Numerous local duplications were found near TEs and included genes involved in host recognition, nutrient utilisation, xenobiotic metabolism, and energy production. Compared with the closely related gall wasp Belonocnema kinseyi, D. kuriphilus has a broader reported distribution and host range and contains higher copy numbers in several gene families associated with chemosensation, detoxification, metabolism, and stress responses. items.title: Benefits of tannin added to concentrate diets fed to ruminants and monogastric livestock
items.authors: J. Caradus
items.abstract: Additives and supplements are often added to concentrate and conserved feeds for both ruminants and monogastrics to maximise feed efficiency, optimise animal health, bridge nutrient deficiencies, and improve economic returns. This may include incorporating polyphenols, such as tannins, extracted from natural plant by-products (e.g., grape pomace or extracts from wattle, quebracho and chestnut trees) to improve animal performance, biohydrogenation processes, quality and quantity of milk and meat, and to reduce methanogenesis. The focus is solely on the use of tannins as an additive—obtained from either extracts or natural variants of feedstuff containing higher amounts of these compounds —and the use of tannins as an additive directly from forages. A review of 72 studies where extracts of, or plants containing, tannins were added to concentrate or conserved feeds for ruminant animals indicated that 63% of cattle/cow studies and 54% of sheep/goat studies confirmed positive benefits. Reasons why benefits were not observed include using the ‘wrong’ type or concentration of tannin, the negation of tannin effects by other compounds in the extract, an unsuitable combination of tannin type and concentrate, or the developmental status of the ruminant. However, assuming this practice continues, this raises the question of whether tannin expression in the main ingredient of concentrate or conserved, feed such as maize or soybean, would be beneficial. For monogastrics, 20 studies for each poultry and swine were reviewed. items.title: Genome-wide analysis of the GATA gene family in Castanea mollissima reveals key regulators involved in salt stress response
items.authors: Xiang-Yu Wang, Xi-Li Liu, Jun Liu, Le Niu, Huo-Qiang Quan, Tong Zhang
items.abstract: The GATA gene family comprises important transcription factors (TFs) that affect plant ontogeny and abiotic/biotic stress tolerance. Castanea mollissima is a significant economic and food-producing tree species in the Northern Hemisphere, known for its strong wind resistance and soil stabilization capabilities. Nevertheless, existing studies have not explored the characteristics and functions of the GATA family in C. mollissima . The study identified 21 CmGATA genes from the N11–1 reference genome assembly of C. mollissima , which were dispersed among 12 chromosomes. Phylogenetic analysis helped to categorize these genes into four distinct subfamilies, with genes belonging to the same subfamily exhibiting considerable similarities in terms of structural characteristics and conserved motif composition. Collinear analysis further revealed that the major driver of CmGATA gene family expansion was segmental duplication, followed by evolutionary pressure predominantly shaped by purifying selection. Phenotypic indicators, such as antioxidant enzyme activity, exhibited significant alterations, and transcriptomic analysis revealed increasingly more differentially expressed genes (DEGs) as salt stress treatment continued. Notably, transcriptome analysis demonstrated the expression patterns of CmGATA genes under salt stress, and combined with their correlation with phenotype indicators and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), effectively benefiting the exploration of the function of CmGATA genes in C. mollissima salt stress response. Additionally, validation experiments utilizing reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) demonstrated gene expression trends consistent with those obtained from RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analyses. items.title: Sustainable development of multifunctional epoxy composites reinforced with jujube seed particles
items.authors: C. Tamilarasan, Rakan Albarakati, C. Raja, N. B. Karthik Babu
items.abstract: This study investigates the multi-functional performance of epoxy composites reinforced with Indian wild jujube ( Ziziphus mauritiana ) seed particles as a sustainable and low-cost reinforcement. Composites were fabricated by hand layup with particle concentrations of 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 wt% in an LY-556 epoxy matrix cured with HY-951 at room temperature. Mechanical, tribological, water absorption, and thermal properties were evaluated, and scanning electron microscopy was used to relate performance to morphology and interfacial behaviour. Particle size analysis showed a bimodal distribution with an average hydrodynamic diameter of 1099 nm and a polydispersity index of 0.969. The composite with 12 wt% particles showed the highest tensile strength of 43.5 MPa, which is a 14.5% improvement over pure epoxy at 38.0 MPa. The maximum flexural strength of 148.7 MPa was obtained at 8 wt% with a 7.5% improvement. Water absorption increased with filler content under both conditions, while saltwater absorption remained lower due to ion-retarded diffusion. Erosion resistance improved for all composites, with the lowest erosion rate of 1.59 mg/min at 20 wt% compared to 1.74 mg/min for pure epoxy. The lowest wear rate of 7.560 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/(Nm) was observed at 4 wt%, after which wear increased with filler content. Thermal analysis showed slower degradation and higher char residue above 450 °C with increasing particle content. This study provides one of the first comprehensive evaluations of epoxy composites reinforced solely with jujube seed particles across mechanical, tribological, and thermal domains. items.title: Influence of Fermentation Methods on Jujube Wine Quality: A Volatile Metabolomics-Based Investigation
items.authors: Bin-Bin Li, Qian Mu, Hui-Jing Guo, Wen-Ting Jia, Ya Liu, Xin-Wen Jin
items.abstract: Co-fermentation with Saccharomyces cerevisiae and selected non-Saccharomyces yeasts is an effective approach for producing fruit wines with distinctive aromas. This study aimed to improve the aroma complexity of jujube wine by evaluating multi-strain sequential inoculation strategies. Two indigenous non-Saccharomyces strains, Hanseniaspora uvarum TD74 and Metschnikowia pulcherrima HJ79, were sequentially inoculated for fermentation in combination with S. cerevisiae. The physicochemical properties and volatile compound profiles of jujube wines produced under different inoculation conditions were analyzed using HS-SPME-GC–MS, coupled with electronic nose, electronic tongue, and chemometric analyses. Compared with single-strain fermentation, sequential inoculation with the two non-Saccharomyces yeasts produced significantly more distinct volatile profiles. In particular, the triple-strain sequential inoculation group (MHS) exhibited higher semi-quantitative levels of most ethyl esters, with a more pronounced fruity aroma in the wine, consistent with the results of sensory analysis. These findings demonstrated that the use of multiple non-Saccharomyces yeasts is an effective strategy for enhancing the aromatic diversity and overall sensory quality of jujube wine, offering a theoretical basis for the rational design of optimized starter cultures for industrial jujube wine production.

items.title: Genome-Wide Identification of the Castanea mollissima MADS-Box Gene Family and Its Potential Roles in Female Flower Development Based on Transcriptomic and Morphological Analyses
items.authors: Liang-Yao Zeng, Xiao-Yan Hu, Hao Yang, Jia Song, Ru-Xin Guo, Haie Zhang
items.abstract: Castanea mollissima is an important woody food crop in China. Late, sparse, and unstable female flower differentiation constrains the development of the chestnut industry. Here, two more-female cultivars, ‘Longquanzhuang No. 2’ (LQ) and ‘Yanqiu’ (YQ), and the control cultivar ‘Yanshanzaofeng’ (ZF) were sampled at five stages after budbreak (7–35 d) for morphological observation and transcriptome sequencing. Morphological divergence became evident at 21 d after budbreak. Transcriptome analysis identified 2223 differentially expressed genes specific to the LQ–ZF comparison at 21 d and 791 inter-cultivar differentially expressed genes shared across 21–35 d. GO enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in transcription factor activity and related pathways. Transcription factor prediction identified MADS-box genes as candidates, and 60 MADS-box members were identified in Chinese chestnut. These comprised 29 Type I members and 31 Type II members, with the latter classified into 13 subfamilies. Integrated analysis of gene-expression patterns and predicted protein interactions showed that more Type II genes were differentially expressed in female flowers and that expression patterns differed between the more-female cultivars and the control. The contrasting expression patterns of putative positive and negative CmMADS regulators may be associated with differences in female flower developmental capacity among these cultivars. RT-qPCR analysis of four representative CmMADS genes showed that genes expressed at higher levels in female flowers generally increased during development, consistent with the transcriptome data. items.title: Persimmon proanthocyanidins-mucins interaction mechanism: structural characteristics, rheological properties, and molecular docking.
items.journal: The Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
items.authors: Ge Z, Zhang X, Zhao Y, Li X, Liu M, Nie R, Zhao G, Wang X.
items.abstract: Background Mucins (MUCs), as the principal constituents of mucus, are closely associated with the transportation and absorption of various bioactive compounds. This study investigated the structural and rheological characteristics of persimmon proanthocyanidin (PPA)-MUC complexes and the interaction mechanism between PPAs and MUCs to elucidate the influence of MUCs on the digestion behavior of PPAs. items.title: Fine-tuning improves deep learning-based digital phenotyping of lettuce genetic resources
items.authors: Eunju Lee, Yuseok Jeong, H. Bae, Yoon-Jung Lee, Seong-Hoon Kim, Young-Wang Na
items.abstract: Morphological characterization of agricultural genetic resources relies largely on visual assessment by experts, and applying the same criteria repeatedly to large collections is labor-intensive. Image-based deep learning can support this process, but systematic evidence on training strategies suited to genebank trait data remains limited. This study targeted six morphological traits of lettuce genetic resources characterized according to the test guidelines of the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV). Using genebank images accumulated from 2012 to 2025, six convolutional neural networks were trained with three training strategies under identical conditions, and their performance was compared. Fine-tuning achieved the highest mean macro F1-score in 35 of the 36 backbone–trait combinations and significantly outperformed training from scratch and feature extraction, whereas no single backbone was superior across all traits. Misclassifications were concentrated in morphologically adjacent classes rather than randomly distributed, and for the ordinal traits, errors spanning two or more class levels were rare. These patterns suggest that the remaining classification difficulty was associated in part with the morphological continuity between neighboring classes. The attainable performance also differed among traits, distinguishing traits for which the training strategy alone achieved relatively high performance from those for which it did not. These results provide empirical evidence for selecting training strategies and for determining the role of model-assisted characterization on a trait-by-trait basis in genebanks.

items.title: Cascading Valorization of Residual Chestnut Biomass: Linking Aqueous Extraction, Reverse Osmosis, Spray Drying, and Solid Reuse
items.authors: Pablo Fernández Santos, Claudia García-Revuelta, Lucía García-Flórez, M. A. González-Arrojo, José Ramón Álvarez Saiz, Susana Luque
items.abstract: Residual chestnut biomass was evaluated in a cascading valorization route combining hot-water extraction, extractant reuse, reverse osmosis (RO), spray drying, and subsequent use of the extracted solid. Two heterogeneous residual Castanea sativa streams were studied at laboratory and pilot scale. Successive extraction at 100 ∘C recovered up to 141 mg gallic acid equivalents (GAE) g−1 dry biomass as Folin-reactive TPC, with 90–93% of the seven-stage response recovered after four fresh-water stages. Reusing the liquid on fresh biomass increased Folin-reactive TPC to 12.0–24.0 mg GAE mL−1. Ultrafiltration did not provide useful fractionation, whereas RO gave >99.9% apparent Folin-reactive TPC retention and 96.5–97.6% total-solids retention; standard batches achieved 86.7–93.5% volume reduction. Carrier-free laboratory spray drying gave a maximum dry-solids collection recovery of approximately 60–62% in the favorable region near 20% feed solids. A representative powder contained 488±27 mg GAE g−1 dry matter, showed a DPPH IC50 of 13.7±1.1μg mL−1, water activity of 0.5850, and a volume-median particle size d50 of 7.42 μm. SEM showed predominantly spherical/sub-spherical particles together with hollow, concave, and partially collapsed particles. Complementary FTIR, MALDI-TOF, SEC-GPC, and qualitative on-flow ESI-MS provided structural and molecular-size fingerprints consistent with chestnut hydrolysable-tannin-related species, while individual assignments remain tentative. After two extraction cycles, residual biomass retained a net calorific value of 18.1–18.2 MJ kg−1 dry basis, although pellet durability decreased. The results define practical trade-offs linking liquid-product recovery and solid-residue valorization in an integrated chestnut-biomass cascade.

items.title: Effects of Different Formulations of Exogenous Nutrient Bag Waste on Soil Properties and Physiological Activities and Root Transcriptomic Responses of Oat
items.authors: Li-Bing Gong, Le Wang, Li-Ping Su, Wei Sa, Quan-Min Dong
items.abstract: This study used typical chestnut soil from Huangyuan County, Qinghai Province as the experimental soil, and selected three oat varieties, “Baiyan 7”, “Qingyan 2”, and “Qinghai 444”, for mixed sowing. A blank control (CK) and five treatments with different ratios of exogenous nutrient bag waste (PF-R-1 to PF-R-5) were established. Through soil physicochemical analysis, microbial biomass determination, RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), the effects of exogenous nutrient bag waste with different ratios soil nutrient availability, microbial activity and root gene expression in oats were systematically evaluated. The results showed that most treatments enhanced soil organic matter, nitrogen content, and microbial activity. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the comparison between PF-R-3 and PF-R-2 treatments exhibited the highest total number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with enrichment in pathways related to ribosomal protein translation, oxidative phosphorylation energy metabolism, and DNA damage repair. These enrichment patterns suggest potential changes in energy metabolism and protein synthesis, although direct functional validation was not performed. Moreover, DEGs uniquely identified in PF-R-3 were significantly enriched in nitrogen metabolism and secondary metabolite biosynthesis pathways; WGCNA identified the coral2 module as the core regulatory module, with its genes predominantly enriched in functions related to transmembrane transport and plant hormone signal transduction, which were highly consistent with efficient root nutrient acquisition and the maintenance of metabolic homeostasis. items.title: Distribution, Development, and Function of Resin Canals in Conifers: Insights from Cellular and Genomic Perspectives.
items.authors: Yi Feng, Shu Diao, Xiao-Hui Lin, Cai-Xia Wang, Xiao-Ping Wang, Yang-Dong Wang
items.abstract: Resin canals are tunnel-like tissue structures primarily responsible for synthesizing and secreting resin. They consist of specialized secondary metabolite-synthesizing epithelial cells and supportive subsidiary cells, which are arranged to form distinctive intercellular spaces. In conifers, resin canals can develop during normal development or be induced by environmental stimuli, which often form an interconnected network and play a crucial role in defense against pathogens and insects. Despite their importance in resin secretion and defense, the mechanisms underlying their formation and function remain poorly understood. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the study of resin canals in conifers from the perspectives of cellular development, defense mechanisms, and molecular regulation. We analyze the distribution patterns, subcellular characteristics and formation and developmental processes of resin canals across different conifer species. Based on studies of traumatic resin canals, we propose a developmental model that depicts the initiation from cambial activity to cell differentiation and canal formation. Furthermore, we focus on resin canal-specific genes and analyze the functions and expression patterns of identified related genes. With the advancement of conifer genome sequencing and single-cell technologies, future research on resin canal regulatory mechanisms and functions is facing unprecedented opportunities. We propose a strategic framework aimed at enhancing conifer breeding, particularly for traits such as stress resilience, disease resistance and wood quality.

items.title: Developmental dynamics of ascorbic acid metabolism in wild jujube fruit: an integrated physiological and transcriptomic analysis.
items.authors: Liu S, Li S, Wang J, He K, Gao S, Liu J.
items.abstract: Wild jujube (Ziziphus jujuba var. spinosa) fruit is rich in ascorbic acid (AsA), but developmental coordination among AsA accumulation, enzyme activities and candidate-gene expression remains unclear. We compared wild jujube with Ziziphus jujuba Mill. cv. 'Lingwuchangzao' grown in the same orchard across five developmental stages. We measured fruit traits, sugars, acids, AsA, total ascorbic acid (T-AsA), dehydroascorbic acid (DHA) and five AsA-related enzyme activities, and analyzed repeated sampling with linear mixed-effects models. Differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), predicted protein-interaction networks and RT-qPCR were applied to 15 wild-jujube RNA-seq samples; ZjVTC2 was transiently overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana. At the young-fruit stage, wild jujube contained 778.75 ± 19.14mg·100g⁻¹ FW AsA and 861.77 ± 17.44mg·100g⁻¹ FW T-AsA. At maturity, AsA content remained higher in wild jujube than in 'Lingwuchangzao' (612.34 ± 13.53 versus 321.22 ± 4.31mg·100g⁻¹ FW). Significant material × developmental-stage interactions occurred for AsA, T-AsA and DHA (P < 0.01). Material differences in DHAR, MDHAR, GalLDH and APX varied by stage, whereas the MIOX interaction was not significant. Transcriptomic and network analyses identified VTC2, GLDH, HXK2, PGMP, and the bHLH gene LOC107430586 as candidates. Transient ZjVTC2 overexpression increased leaf AsA by 72.65% (P < 0.01). Thus, AsA accumulation differed between materials in a stage-dependent manner, and ZjVTC2 was functionally supported, whereas the other candidate genes require validation.

items.title: Comparative Structural, Optical, Morphological and Elemental Characterisation of Jujube-Mediated Silver and Zinc Oxide Nanoparticles
items.authors: H. M. Umar, Jamilatu Sumaila, T. Zangina
items.abstract: Plant extracts offer a practical route for nanoparticle synthesis because naturally occurring compounds can participate in particle formation and remain associated with the resulting material. In this study, jujube extract was used to prepare silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) and zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs). Both products were examined using the same set of characterization techniques: X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), ultraviolet-visible (UV–Vis) spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). The XRD results clearly differentiated the two materials. The Ag sample showed peaks at approximately 38.27°, 44.45°, 64.55°, and 77.57°, characteristic of face-centered-cubic Ag, while the ZnO sample displayed reflections at 31.91°, 34.55°, 36.38°, 47.60°, 56.78°, and 63.02°, consistent with hexagonal wurtzite ZnO. FTIR spectra from both samples contained bands associated with plant-derived functional groups, along with low-wavenumber features related to their respective inorganic phases. Their optical responses were also distinct. Ag showed the characteristic response of metallic nanoparticles, whereas ZnO exhibited an optical edge at about 392.5 nm, corresponding to approximately 3.16 eV. This value was calculated from the optical-edge wavelength and is not presented as a formal Tauc band gap. SEM images showed rough, uneven, and strongly aggregated surfaces in both samples. EDX further showed strong Ag signals in the silver sample and Zn and O as the main detected elements in the ZnO sample. Overall, the study compares two different nanomaterials produced using the same jujube-based approach and shows how their structural, optical, morphological, and elemental characteristics differ.

items.title: Density Estimation in Heritage Timber Elements Using Resistograph Drilling Resistance
items.authors: Yilién Cabrera Martín, C. Baggio, Silvia Santini, G. Íñiguez-González
items.abstract: Accurate structural diagnosis of timber elements in historic buildings requires minimally invasive and operationally reliable assessment methods compatible with heritage conservation principles. This study aims to estimate timber density in situ directly from Resistograph drilling resistance. To achieve this objective, density estimates derived from Woodpecker impact penetration tests were paired with Resistograph drilling resistance measurements through a mesh to develop a point to point correspondence and calibrate a linear model relating density to drilling resistance and enabling its direct application through Resistograph measurements. The database comprised thirteen historic sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa Mill.) beams from the Cloister of Michelangelo in the Baths of Diocletian complex, Rome, Italy. Statistical analyses included the assessment of multiple window sizes, segmented penetration intervals, model calibration, and Leave-One-Beam-Out (LOBO) cross validation. The resulting model enables density estimation using only Resistograph measurements and demonstrated high predictive accuracy, achieving a coefficient of determination of 92%.

items.title: Post-harvest treatments to reduce emergence and damage caused by larvae of Curculio sayi (Coleoptera: Curculionidae).
items.authors: Ferguson M, Guyer DE, McCullough DG.
items.abstract: Damage caused by lesser chestnut weevil (Curculio sayi Gyllenhal) larval feeding affects yield and marketability of chestnuts (Castanea spp.) produced by commercial growers and hobbyists across the eastern United States. Post-harvest treatments to mitigate weevil damage involve submerging chestnuts in heated water for ≥20 min. Prolonged submergence in hot water, however, can discolor chestnuts or diminish quality of chestnuts in cold storage. We assessed larval emergence from chestnuts held at room temperature (controls), or submerged in water at 22.5°C (unheated), 43.3°C, 49.0°C, 54.4°C, or 60°C for periods of 5 to 30 min. Subsets of treated chestnuts were quartered after submergence, then again following 30, 60, or 90 d of cold storage (1°C) to evaluate larval feeding damage, chestnut quality and storability. Effective control (less than 1 emerged larva per 100 chestnuts) corresponded to submergence for 15 min in 49°C water, 10 min in 54.4°C water or 5 min in 60°C water, while 24 to 41 larvae per 100 chestnuts emerged from controls. Quality of chestnuts in cold storage declined sharply for chestnuts submerged in 54.4°C water for 25 min or 60°C water for 20 to 25 min. Submerging chestnuts for 10 to 20 min in 54.4°C water appeared optimal; no larvae emerged and chestnut quality was retained for 60 d in cold storage. Time needed to attain core temperatures lethal to weevil larvae varied with chestnut size. Curatura (water curing) and exposure to alternating cycles of warm and cold temps were also evaluated.

items.title: ZJP-2, a novel wild jujube polysaccharide, enhances longevity, cognitive function, and mitigates oxidative stress via mitochondrial regulation in Caenorhabditis elegans.
items.authors: Shakir MZ, Ullah I, Usmani MW, Ning J, Liu J, Zhou X, Zhao Y, Du Q, Chen H, Ali M, Wang N, Liu X.
items.abstract: Oxidative stress, caused by an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defenses, drives aging and age related functional decline. Natural polysaccharides from medicinal plants are promising interventions against oxidative stress related disorders. This study examined the protective effects of a novel polysaccharide (ZJP-2) isolated from wild jujube (Ziziphus jujuba Mill. var. spinosa) against stress induced physiological deterioration in Caenorhabditis elegans. Using lipopolysaccharide exposure, heat shock, and oxidative stress models, we assessed ZJP-2 effects on lifespan, health span, antioxidant capacity, and stress response pathways. ZJP-2 (0.25-1 mg/mL) showed no toxicity and did not inhibit Escherichia coli OP50 growth. Treatment significantly improved locomotor activity, pharyngeal pumping, and reproductive capacity. The optimal dose increased average lifespan by 42.03% and reduced intestinal lipofuscin accumulation by 52.89%. Under heat stress (37 °C), ZJP-2 enhanced thermotolerance and improved survival under oxidative stress. Intracellular ROS levels decreased in a dose dependent manner, accompanied by reductions in malondialdehyde and increases in superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione activities. Gene expression analysis revealed modulation of antioxidant and mitochondrial-associated genes, along with p38 MAPK-associated genes. ZJP-2 also promoted activation of the longevity associated transcription factor daf-16. These findings demonstrate that ZJP-2 enhances stress resistance, reduces oxidative damage, and promotes a healthy lifespan, highlighting its potential as a natural bioactive compound to mitigate stress related aging.

items.title: Comparative analysis of plastomes of Rubus cultivars and development of molecular markers for species delimitation.
items.authors: Hu L, Wu Y, Zhao Z, Wu W, Cao F, Wang Z, Li W.
items.abstract: Key message Plastome analyses confirmed the taxonomic classification of cultivated Rubus and identified candidate InDel markers for distinguishing major cultivated groups, offering genetic resources for future studies of hybrid identification and breeding. The genus Rubus, belonging to the Rosaceae family, comprises numerous wild germplasm resources. Among its most economically valuable cultivars are red raspberry, black raspberry, blackberry, as well as raspberry × blackberry hybrids. In this study, we assembled and characterized 81 newly Rubus plastomes, including 22 wild species and 59 cultivars. All genomes exhibited the typical quadripartite structure, with sizes ranging from 155,385 to 157,012 bp and containing 130 annotated genes (113 unique functional genes), indicating a high degree of conservation in plastome architecture and gene order. A comparative analysis was further conducted using plastomes from 16 representative Rubus cultivars, representing all unique plastome sequences. The repeat sequences, codon usage bias, and hypervariable regions were systematically analyzed. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that modern Rubus cultivars primarily cluster within three subgenera: Rubus, Idaeobatus, and Melanobatus, with black raspberry phylogenetically placed within Melanobatus. Furthermore, four InDel markers were developed and validated for distinguishing three Rubus cultivar groups (black raspberry, red raspberry and hybrids). In summary, our research substantially expands available plastome resources for Rubus species and cultivars, thereby facilitating species delimitation and supporting future hybrid breeding.

items.title: Genome-wide analysis of cork oak NLRs reveals RNL-associated duplications and immune receptor candidates associated with biotic and abiotic stress response
items.authors: L. M. Gonçalves, M. Oliveira, P. Barros
items.abstract: The Nucleotide-Binding Domain Leucine-Rich Repeat (NLR) gene family is a central component of plant immune systems, yet its diversity and evolutionary dynamics remain poorly characterized in long-lived tree species. Here, we performed a genome-wide analysis of the NLR gene repertoire in Quercus suber (cork oak) using a newly developed annotation tool–InterNLR–which identifies and classifies NLRs as canonical and non-canonical. We identified a total of 374 canonical NLRs, and 544 non-canonical NLRs–which may represent pseudogenes, gene fragments or evolutionary intermediates. Phylogenetic analyses based on the NB-ARC domain highlighted the distinct evolutionary trajectory of RNL proteins, which function as “helper” NLRs and show evidence of clade-specific gene duplication. Transcriptomic analyses revealed significant differences in gene-level expression among NLR classes in cork oak stem tissues, mainly driven by contrasts involving the non-canonical N class. Seven cork oak NLR genes, sharing putative orthology with abiotic stress-responsive NLRs found in other species, were also differentially expressed in stems under drought conditions. From these, four candidate NLRs arise as candidate components of shared or convergent responses to drought and P. cinnamomi infection. Population-genetic analyses of RNA-seq-derived variants from expressed NLR loci in two Iberian populations further revealed heterogeneous patterns among expressed NLR loci, with a predominance of positive Tajima’s D values. Together, these results provide new insights into the evolution, expression, and functional diversification of NLRs in cork oak. This work advances our understanding of immune gene architecture in an ecologically and economically important forest tree species.

items.title: Molecular Characterization and Evolutionary Relationships of WRKYs in Five Rubus Species and Functional Analysis of RiWRKY48 in Rubus idaeus
items.authors: Zhuang Wen, Jian-Xin Fan, Yao Jiang, Qin Yang, Xue-Jiao Cao
items.abstract: WRKY transcription factors play crucial roles in plant growth, development, and stress responses. However, their systematic evolution and functions within the genus Rubus remain incompletely understood. In this study, genome-wide identification, evolutionary analysis and functional characterization of the WRKY gene family were conducted in five Rubus species. A total of 37–67 members were identified and classified into three groups by phylogenetic analysis. The collinearity result, gene family expansion and contraction analyses revealed a contraction trend within the Rubus lineage compared with the outgroup sweet cherry. Promoter cis-acting element analysis predicted widespread involvement of these genes in hormone and stress responses. Expression profiling revealed tissue-specific patterns among WRKY genes, with most members down-regulated during fruit development and differentially regulated by biotic and abiotic stresses. Further correlation analysis and experimental validation were focused on RiWRKY48 in red raspberry (Rubus idaeus L.). This protein was localized to the nucleus and lacked transcriptional activation activity. Combined in silico modeling (AlphaFold3) and dual-luciferase reporter assays revealed that RiWRKY48 may repressed the promoter activity of RiUFGT4, a key anthocyanin biosynthetic gene, suggesting a putative interaction with the W-box element. In summary, this study systematically characterized the evolutionary features of the Rubus WRKY family and provided evidence for a potential regulatory role of RiWRKY48 in anthocyanin biosynthesis through modulation of RiUFGT4 promoter activity. These findings provided new insights into the regulatory roles of WRKY transcription factors in fruit quality development in Rubus species.

items.title: Chestnut-quebracho tannins shape the fecal metabolome of weaned pigs through microbiota-dependent urolithin production.
items.journal: Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology
items.authors: Correa F, Luise D, Palumbo F, Scicchitano D, Rampelli S, Molino S, Panciroli N, Candela M, Garay-Mayol B, Ávila-Gálvez MÁ, González-Sarrías A, Castagnetti A, Trevisi P.
items.abstract: Background Chestnut and quebracho tannins may support gut health in weaned piglets, but their efficacy likely depends on farm environment and microbial capacity to convert tannins into bioactive metabolites. This study evaluated the effects of a blend of chestnut-derived hydrolysable tannins and quebracho-derived condensed tannins on growth performance, diarrhea occurrence, gut metagenome, and fecal metabolome in piglets reared under two commercial farm conditions. A total of 160 weaned piglets (initial body weight 6.53 ± 0.13 kg) were assigned to a 2 × 2 factorial design comprising 2 weaning units (W1 and W2) and 2 dietary treatments (control diet or control diet + 2 g/kg tannin blend; 40 piglets per treatment × farm). The trial lasted 76 d, with weighings at T0 (entry into weaning, median 28 d), T1 (d 35), T2 (d 49), and T3 (d 76). Fecal scores and samples were collected at T1, T2, and T3 for shotgun metagenomics (155 samples per time point) and untargeted metabolomics, and targeted urolithin quantification was performed in tannin-treated piglets at T1 and T2. Results Tannin supplementation did not affect overall growth performance throughout the weaning phase, but reduced diarrhea occurrence at T2 in W2 (P = 0.032). Species-level beta diversity was consistently affected by treatment across time points (R 2 = 0.01-0.03; P Conclusions Overall, chestnut-quebracho tannins were associated with a farm-dependent reduction in post-weaning diarrhea and modulated the gut ecosystem through microbiota-dependent polyphenol metabolism.

items.title: Strain identification, probiotic potential evaluation, and mannanase production optimisation of <i>Lactiplantibacillus plantarum</i> HDM10.
items.authors: Huang L, Yang R, Li Z, Yang S, Zhao D.
items.abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum ( L. plantarum ) HDM10, isolated from fermented winter jujube ( Ziziphus jujuba ) juice, was identified by biochemical and molecular analyses. The strain exhibited γ-haemolysis, susceptibility to several tested antibiotics, and strong gastrointestinal tolerance, with survival rates of 72.63% and 80.00% at pH 2.0 and 3.0, respectively. Survival remained above 70% in 0.05-0.5% bile salts and reached 67.82% at 1.0%. More than 80% of cells survived simulated gastric and intestinal conditions. Response surface methodology optimised mannanase production to 87.73 U/mL, representing a 27.1% increase over the initial activity. Congo red staining confirmed enhanced polysaccharide hydrolysis. HDM10 also showed strong mucin adhesion (>70%) and slight growth promotion in the presence of mucin. These results demonstrate its safety, probiotic potential, and suitability for -synbiotic applications.

items.title: Chestnut flour-enriched bread reduces postprandial glycaemic response in healthy adults: a randomised, controlled crossover study.
items.authors: Houghton MJ, Peiris DR, Sulaimani N, Visvanathan R, Nicolotti L, Cardoso BR.
items.abstract: Elevated postprandial glycaemic excursions contribute to cardiometabolic disease risk, highlighting the importance of dietary strategies to attenuate postprandial glycaemia for prevention. Chestnut ( Castanea spp.) is rich in dietary fibre, resistant starch and bioactive (poly)phenols that may modulate carbohydrate digestion, yet evidence in human studies remains limited. We investigated the effects of a chestnut flour-enriched bread on postprandial glycaemic and insulinaemic responses in healthy adults. In a randomised crossover trial, fourteen healthy participants consumed isocaloric meals providing 50 g available carbohydrate as either chestnut flour-enriched bread (50% chestnut flour/50% wheat flour) or control bread (100% wheat flour), following an overnight fast. Capillary blood glucose and insulin were measured over 180 min, and incremental area under the curve (iAUC) was assessed for each. The (poly)phenol composition of the wheat and chestnut flours and the control (wheat only) and chestnut flour-enriched breads was characterised using RP-HPLC-HRFTMS. Chestnut flour-enriched bread, containing (+)-catechin, myricetin, gallic, gentisic and p -coumaric acids (∼480 mg total (poly)phenols), significantly reduced glucose iAUC by 27% compared with control bread (∼100 mg total (poly)phenols) ( p = 0.0319, paired t-test; main effects of the meal: p = 0.0243, ANOVA). Glucose concentrations were 16% lower at 120 min ( p = 0.0131) and 14% lower at 150 min ( p = 0.0071). Total insulin exposure did not differ between the meals, but chestnut enrichment reduced the insulin peak time by approximately 24 min ( p = 0.0430). Partial substitution of wheat flour for chestnut flour in bread significantly attenuated postprandial glycaemia in healthy adults, mainly by lowering late-pha…

items.title: Humus content and group composition in rainfed soil of southeastern Kazakhstan under the influence of fertilizers in a grain crop rotation
items.authors: V. Gusev, S. Kenenbayev, E. Zhusupbekov, K. Rustemova
items.abstract: The aim of the study was to assess the effect of manure, straw, and mineral fertilizers on the humus content and fractional composition of humus in light chestnut soil under a rainfed grain crop rotation in southeastern Kazakhstan. It was found that organic fertilizers had a more pronounced positive effect on the humus status of the soil than the mineral fertilizer system. The most distinct effect was observed after manure application under winter wheat, where humus content increased from 1.67–1.70% to 1.74%. Straw incorporation had a more moderate and not always statistically significant effect on humus content, increasing it from 1.68% to 1.70%. The application of mineral fertilizers did not cause significant changes in this indicator compared with the control. The effect of fertilizers on the fractional composition of humus was less pronounced than their effect on total humus content. The most noticeable changes were recorded under manure application, where the Cha/Cfa ratio decreased to 0.72 compared with 0.74 in the control. It was shown that under rainfed farming conditions, manure is the most effective factor for maintaining the humus status of the soil, while the changes identified at the initial stage of fertilizer application may be regarded as indicators of the direction of subsequent organic matter transformation under the long-term application of organic materials.

items.title: Effect of the combined application of biological products and mineral fertilizers on soil agrochemical properties and spring barley productivity under the conditions of the Zhetysu region
items.authors: S. Tanirbergenov, K. Tynybayeva, S. Bazarbayev, M. Zhumagulova, Zh. P. Bimurza, M. Tulegenova
items.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of mineral fertilizers and biological products on the agrochemical properties of light chestnut soil and the productivity of spring barley under rainfed conditions in the Zhetysu Region, Kazakhstan. The objective was to assess the effects of different fertilization systems on soil agrochemical properties, plant growth, and grain yield of spring barley. The field experiment was conducted with three replicates using a mineral fertilizer background of N 60 P 90 K 80 and four biological products - BioEcoGum, BIOGRANO forte, BioAzoPhashit, and BioPhos - applied either alone or in combination with mineral fertilizers. Soil total humus, nitrate nitrogen, easily hydrolysable nitrogen, available phosphorus, exchangeable potassium, carbonates, and soil reaction were determined, along with plant growth parameters and grain yield. Fertilizer application had no substantial effect on total humus content or soil reaction but was associated with changes in the concentrations of available nutrients. The highest nitrate nitrogen (24.0 mg/kg) and available phosphorus (26.5 mg/kg) contents were recorded with N 60 P 90 K 80 + BioAzoPhashit. The greatest plant height (51.3±1.1 cm) was observed with N 60 P 90 K 80 + BioEcoGum. The highest grain yield (1.13 t/ha) and a statistically significant yield increase over the untreated control (0.33 t/ha, or 41.2%) were obtained with N 60 P 90 K 80 + BIOGRANO forte. When applied alone, the biological products produced grain yields ranging from 0.887 to 0.956 t/ha, with yield increases over the control not exceeding the least significant d ifference. Statistical analysis confirmed a significant effect of mineral fertilization on spring barley grain yield, whereas no significant additional effect of the biological produc…

items.title: Assessing Botanical Authenticity of Honey Through DNA-Metabarcoding-Based Pollen Analysis: A Preliminary Study
items.authors: Lucia Ranieri, Roberta Piredda, A. Mottola, Chiara Intermite, Martina Denami, Lucilia Lorusso
items.abstract: Honey is highly vulnerable to botanical mislabeling and fraud, highlighting the need for dedicated analytical approaches capable of reliably supporting authenticity assessment. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to integrate traditional melissopalynology and rbcL DNA metabarcoding for the botanical characterization of honeys collected from Apulian beekeepers. Melissopalynological analysis confirmed the labeled floral source in 6/10 (60%) samples, while four samples were reclassified. One cherry honey was identified as polyfloral, and one robinia (acacia) honey as crimson clover honey. The two samples labeled as polyfloral showed a predominance of chestnut and coriander pollen. In contrast, molecular results confirmed label declarations for chestnut and cherry honeys, whereas robinia (acacia) honeys highlighted known limitations associated with under-represented pollen taxa. In terms of biodiversity, DNA metabarcoding identified 128 plant families, whereas melissopalynology detected only 42. Despite this difference in taxonomic resolution, both approaches converged on the core botanical composition of the honey matrix, sharing 39 plant families that represent the principal nectariferous and entomophilous taxa. Overall, melissopalynology proved decisive for regulatory label verification, while DNA metabarcoding provided a broader qualitative description of the botanical composition. As a preliminary pilot study, the combined application of melissopalynology and DNA metabarcoding may contribute to a more comprehensive assessment of honey botanical origin and traceability; however, molecular detection alone cannot be considered sufficient to establish compliance with legal requirements for unifloral honey labeling.

items.title: A collaborative perception framework for green jujube: from lightweight key point detection to posture-aware harvest analysis
items.authors: Hong-Yan Zhu, Run-Long Cao, Shuai Qin, Cheng-Zhi Lin, Wei-Zhen Sun, Yan-Li Zou
items.abstract: Automated harvesting is pivotal to smart agriculture, yet precisely localizing picking points in complex orchard environments remains a key challenge for robotic harvesting systems. To this end, this study proposes a collaborative perception framework integrating a lightweight pose estimation model termed RepViT-DSConv-ARC-PoseHead enhanced YOLO (RDA-YOLO) with Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2). RDA-YOLO is the lightweight component responsible for real-time fruit detection and keypoint localization, while SAM2 is adopted for fruit contour segmentation and occlusion assessment. Based on the YOLOv11n-POSE architecture, we introduce Distribution Shift Convolution (DSConv) to reduce computational overhead and design the C3k2_RepViT module to enhance multi-scale feature fusion. Crucially, a specialized Adaptive Regression Coordination Pose Head (ARC-PoseHead) is developed to replace traditional prediction structures, employing log-scale polar regression and subpixel refinement to significantly improve coordinate perception of jujubes and key points under complex backgrounds. RDA-YOLO performs real-time detection and locates key points such as the pedicel-fruit transition zone to calculate optimal harvesting angles, while SAM2 performs fine-grained contour segmentation based on detection boxes to determine occlusion status and establish harvesting priority. Experimental results show that RDA-YOLO achieves 93.9% precision and 94.9% mAP@50 for green jujube detection, while for key point detection, it attains a superior precision of 90.4% and a mAP@50 of 83.6%. Notably, the model achieves a lightweight design by reducing parameters to 2.490 million and computational load to 5.7 GFLOPs. Deployment feasibility was verified on the field robot control computer and a robotic platform …

items.title: In vitro antioxidant evaluation of a herbal formulation containing sesame root (Sesamum indicum L.) and raspberry (Rubus idaeus L.)
items.authors: R. Gomathi, Maheswari T. N. Uma, K. Rajesh
items.abstract: Oxidative stress causes tissue damage, persistent inflammation and slowed wound healing. There is growing interest in plant-based antioxidants as safer substitutes for synthetic ones. Rich in lignans and polyphenols, sesame (Sesamum indicum L.) and raspberry (Rubus idaeus L.) have been shown to possess cytoprotective and free-radical-scavenging properties important for tissue protection. To develop an aqueous sesame–raspberry herbal formulation and evaluate its in vitro antioxidant potential using 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), hydrogen peroxide (H2O₂) scavenging and ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays. The roots of R. idaeus and S. indicum were cleaned, dried in the shade, ground into a powder and extracted separately with distilled water under controlled heating conditions. The extracts were oven-dried and combined in equal amounts to prepare the herbal formulation. The final dry extract yield was 10.46 %. Preliminary phytochemical screening was performed and the antioxidant activity of the formulation was evaluated using DPPH, H2O2 scavenging and FRAP assays at concentrations of 10–50 µg/mL, with ascorbic acid as the reference standard. Preliminary phytochemical screening revealed abundant flavonoids and phenols, moderate levels of alkaloids, tannins, glycosides, terpenoids and anthocyanins and the presence of saponins and steroids. The herbal formulation demonstrated concentration-dependent antioxidant activity, with responses ranging 62.25–89.99 % in the DPPH assay, 47.30–84.45 % in the H₂O₂ assay and 67.41–87.62 % in the FRAP assay across 10–50 µg/mL. The formulation showed lower antioxidant responses than the ascorbic acid standard across the tested concentrations. The aqueous sesame–raspberry herbal formulation demonstrated measurable in vitro…

items.title: Recurrent Invasion of Oregon's Coastal Forests by the Sudden Oak Death Pathogen: The NA2 Lineage's First Escape into the Wild.
items.authors: Chase SM, Søndreli KL, Grünwald NJ, LeBoldus JM.
items.abstract: Phytophthora ramorum , the sudden oak death (SOD) pathogen, has invaded U.S. nurseries and western forests repeatedly. Invasions by three distinct clonal lineages (NA1, NA2, and EU1) have affected U.S. wildland forests since 2001. Most recently, NA2 established an invasive population in coastal forests surrounding Port Orford in southwest Oregon. This is the first instance of NA2 encountered outside of a nursery. We assessed this new invasion's diversity and population structure using single-nucleotide polymorphisms from whole-genome sequences of 195 isolates. Genomes were sampled from the nursery trade and from the forest invasion surrounding Port Orford. The NA2 forest invasion lacks genetic diversity and likely originated from a single introduction. A subset of NA2 isolates (10.8%) were genetically distant from all other isolates including each other. This distance was correlated with frequency of genomic runs of homozygosity. No evidence of hybridization was found, though NA2 and EU1 mating types are compatible and their ranges in wild forests overlap. The aggressiveness and sporulation of NA2 isolates were measured on three host tree species and compared with isolates of other lineages. NA2 and EU1 phenotypes were similar. NA2 caused larger lesions on Douglas-fir and tanoak seedlings than NA1, the lineage of the original introduction into Oregon forests. Results indicate that the NA2 population is not distinct from the older EU1 Oregon population in terms of population diversity, disease aggressiveness, or potential for spread. However, the introduction of NA2 has increased the SOD epidemic's range, risk of hybridization, overall genetic diversity, and adaptive potential.

items.title: Hyperoside Derived from Actinidia arguta Bee Pollen Alleviates Zearalenone-Induced Hepatotoxicity and Oxidative Stress in Piglets via the PI3K/AKT Signaling Pathway
items.journal: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
items.authors: Nan-Nan Liu, Dong-Fei You, Yun-Fei Jiang, Tian-Yu Han, Guang-Liang Shi
items.abstract: Zearalenone (ZEA) is a prevalent mycotoxin inducing hepatotoxic effects. Hyperoside (HYP), a flavonoid derived from Actinidia arguta bee pollen, exhibits hepatoprotective properties against ZEA; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying this protection remain incompletely characterized. This study integrated in vivo piglet models, in vitro porcine hepatocytes, network pharmacology, and molecular docking to characterize the molecular targets of HYP. The results demonstrated that HYP significantly attenuated ZEA-induced hepatic lesions and oxidative stress. Computational analyses pinpointed the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway as the core target of HYP. In vitro validation revealed that HYP phenocopied the AKT activator SC79 in suppressing ZEA-induced hepatocyte apoptosis, an efficacy partially abrogated by the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. Conclusively, HYP ameliorates ZEA-induced hepatotoxicity by activating the PI3K/AKT axis to mitigate oxidative stress and apoptosis, underscoring its translational potential as a functional detoxifying additive for food and feed applications.

items.title: pH-Responsive Chitosan–Alginate Hydrogel Beads Co-Encapsulating Jujube Polysaccharides and cAMP: Enhanced Antioxidant Activity and Gastrointestinal Controlled Release
items.authors: Guang-Hui Zhao, Chi Han, Wei-Hua Wang, Jian-Kang Lu, Chun-Lan Zhang, Khan Nazeer
items.abstract: Jujube polysaccharides (ZJPA) and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) are bioactive compounds with antioxidant and health-promoting potential, and their combination exhibits enhanced antioxidant activity. However, their limited stability and susceptibility to gastrointestinal environmental stresses restrict their applications in functional foods. In this study, a pH-responsive composite hydrogel bead delivery system was developed using chitosan (CS) and sodium alginate (SA) as wall materials to co-encapsulate ZJPA and cAMP, aiming to protect these bioactive compounds during gastrointestinal digestion while maintaining their enhanced functionality. The hydrogel beads were fabricated via the ionotropic gelation method, and the formulation parameters were optimized using single-factor experiments combined with response surface methodology (RSM). The optimized hydrogel beads were obtained under the conditions of calcium chloride concentration of 3%, CS concentration of 0.5%, SA concentration of 3%, and core-to-wall ratio of 1:6, with a cAMP microencapsulation yield (MEY) of 97.79%. Structural characterization confirmed that ZJPA and cAMP were successfully incorporated into the CS-SA network through electrostatic interactions and intermolecular hydrogen bonding without the formation of new covalent bonds. Furthermore, the hydrogel beads exhibited distinct pH-responsive swelling and gastrointestinal release behaviors, providing effective protection under acidic gastric conditions and enabling sustained release under intestinal conditions. Importantly, the DPPH radical scavenging assay demonstrated that the co-encapsulation strategy preserved the enhanced antioxidant activity between ZJPA and cAMP. items.title: Integrated UHPLC-MS/MS Metabolomics, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and Experimental Validation Reveal the Anti-Inflammatory Mechanisms of Pyrus pyrifolia Peel Extract
items.authors: Ducdat Le, D. Rhyu, Mi-Na Lee
items.abstract: Pyrus pyrifolia (Burm. f.) Nakai has long been utilized in traditional East Asian medicine to treat respiratory disorders, fever, cough, and inflammatory conditions. This study aimed to evaluate the antioxidative and anti-inflammatory effects of P. pyrifolia. UHPLC-MS/MS analysis revealed that P. pyrifolia contained 22 primary and other putative compounds belonging to diverse phytochemical groups—phenolics, flavonoids, fatty acids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and other compounds. Network pharmacology identified a subset of overlapping targets associated with inflammatory diseases, which were significantly enriched in immune- and inflammation-related biological processes. KEGG pathway analysis demonstrated that the Toll-like receptor was the principal pathway potentially regulated by overlapping targets. PPI network analysis revealed TNF to be the most influential hub target, which was verified by molecular docking analysis. Interestingly, the P. pyrifolia extract significantly inhibited LPS-induced TNF-α production by modulating IκBα phosphorylation and restoring IκBα expression in the NF-κB signaling pathway. Additionally, the P. pyrifolia extract also markedly reduced the phosphorylation of ERK, p38, and JNK, thereby affecting MAPK signaling pathways. Our findings provide mechanistic evidence supporting the traditional medicinal use of P. pyrifolia to establish a theoretical framework to develop phytopharmaceuticals for inflammatory diseases.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of adenine cytokinins and diphenylurea derivatives during in vitro clonal micropropagation of raspberry cultivars Karamelka and Octavia
items.authors: N. Solovykh
items.abstract: Red raspberry (Rubus idaeusL.) exhibits cultivar-specific requirements for nutrient medium composition duringin vitroclonal micropropagation. Therefore, research aimed at optimizing micropropagation protocols for promising cultivars remains relevant. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various cytokinins at the multiplication stagein vitro for the cultivars Karamelka and Octavia. For the first time, a comparative assessment was conducted on the effects of plant growth regulators from the adenine and diphenylurea groups on the micropropagation process. Microcuttings were cultured on MS medium supplemented with 0.1 mg/L β-indole-3-butyric acid (IBA), 0.5 mg/L gibberellic acid (GA), and one of the cytokinins tested. The study employed adenine-type cytokinins: kinetin, zeatin, N⁶-(Δ²-isopentenyl)adenine (2iP), and 6-benzylaminopurine (BAP) at concentrations ranging from 0.6 to 1.8 mg/L, as well as diphenylurea derivatives: thidiazuron (TDZ) and forchlorfenuron (CPPU) at concentrations of 0.06–0.18 mg/L. Among the adenine group, 2iP proved to be the least effective, while kinetin yielded low multiplication coefficients: 1.56 (Octavia) and 2.03 (Karamelka). These cytokinins cannot be recommended for cloning the studied raspberry cultivars. In the presence of BAP (0.6–0.9 mg/L), multiplication coefficients reached 3.67 (cv. Karamelka) and 4.26 (cv. Octavia), with the proportion of shoots at least 20 mm in length amounting to 45.32–49.33% and 60.33–64.67%, respectively. items.title: Engineering lignin-tannin nanoassemblies for multifunctional and sustainable skincare.
items.authors: Gordobil O, Kathpal T, Gonet-Surówka A, Brzychczy-Włoch M, Diaz RH, Peña-Rodriguez C.
items.abstract: Lignin is increasingly recognized as a sustainable raw material for the development of safe and multifunctional cosmetic ingredients. Nanoengineering strategies enable its transformation into uniform colloidal particles with improved dispersibility and functionality. However, reducing its intense color without compromising its intrinsic bioactivity remains a major challenge for cosmetic applications. In this work, a function-preserving particle design strategy was developed by synergistically combining lignin with tannins at the nanoscale to create fully biobased phenolic colloidal assemblies. Four lignin-tannin colloidal systems (LTPs) were synthetized by combining softwood and hardwood kraft lignins with commercial tannins from chestnut and mimosa at different lignin-to-tannin ratios using an antisolvent precipitation method. The influence of polyphenolic components and processing conditions on particle size, morphology, and functionality was investigated. The resulting LTPs exhibited controlled particle dimensions in the range of 150-500 nm, together with superior multifunctional protective properties and improved aesthetic compatibility for skincare applications. Compared to colloidal lignin particles, LTPs showed improved antioxidant activity (75% reduction in IC₅₀), highly tunable UV-shielding capacity, and enhanced antibacterial effectiveness against Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Cutibacterium acnes, with minimum bactericidal concentrations (MBC) values between 0.77 and 2.48 mg/mL, while maintaining acceptable cytocompatibility depending on the particle composition at relatively high concentrations. items.title: Joint species distribution modelling for restoration of American chestnut ( Castanea dentata ) in the United States under current and future climate conditions
items.authors: Matthew E. Fertakos, Bethany A. Bradley, J. Doser, M. Itter
items.abstract: American chestnut ( Castanea dentata ) was once a dominant tree species spanning the eastern temperate forests of the United States until the introduction of chestnut blight in the early twentieth century resulted in its functional extinction. Recent advances in the development of blight‐resistant American chestnut could support widespread restoration, but optimal locations for restoration plantings remain uncertain. Previous models of American chestnut created to address this question rely on post‐blight occurrence data and pseudo‐absences which likely underrepresent its distribution. They also omit abundance information, which may be critical for identifying successful restoration sites. Additionally, climate change is shifting the locations of suitable habitat for eastern temperate trees like American chestnut, complicating long‐term restoration planning. We use a Bayesian joint species distribution modelling (JSDM) framework to jointly model current and future suitability for 11 chestnut‐associated tree species within a broader assemblage of 39 tree species commonly found in eastern temperate forests. We identified a poleward shift in habitat for the forest communities American chestnut historically occurred with. Especially suitable areas were in the northeastern United States and northern Michigan, as well as possible refugia in higher elevation areas of the Appalachian Mountains. These areas overlap with 2988 existing conservation properties most suitable for restoration. Synthesis and applications . Our joint species distribution modelling approach highlights its value in guiding the adaptive restoration of functionally extinct species in forests shaped by past and ongoing disturbance. items.title: Investigation of Dark Adsorption Conditions for Textile Dyestuffs Removal Using Horse Chestnut‐Based Mesoporous Activated Carbons in Aqueous Media
items.authors: Veli Şimşek, R. Z. Yarbay, H. Sayğılı
items.abstract: This study investigated the dark adsorption (DA) behavior of the textile dyes(TEDs) Methyl Orange (MO) and Methylene Blue (MB) onto porous activated carbons (PACs) synthesized via a carbonization–activation process. PACs were obtained using the carbonization/activation synthesis method. To synthesize PACs, Horse chestnut ( Aesculushippocastanum L .) as a precursor, and two different activating agents (ZnCl2 and K2CO3) were used. The synthesis of PACs was carried out in different ratios (1:1, 1:5, and 1:10; biomass/agent). The physicochemical characteristics of feedstock and PACs were determined by BET, FT‐IR, SEM/EDX, MAPPING, and XRD. Batch sorption studies were performed to compare the selected anionic and cationic TEDs. The removal of MO and MB was over 97% after 15 min, 0.005–0.01 g, and at the solution pH. The maximum qe values for 100 ppm MB and MO TEDs solution were calculated as 99.8 and 196.6 mg/g, respectively. Furthermore, comprehensive equilibrium, kinetic, and thermodynamic analyses of MO adsorption onto HCACZ5 and HCACK5 were conducted to elucidate the adsorption characteristics, rate‐controlling mechanism, and thermodynamic nature of the process. The results demonstrated that temperature exerted a distinct influence on the adsorption behavior of the two adsorbents, resulting in different responses.

items.title: A novel Cryphonectria species (Cryphonectriaceae, Diaporthales) discovered on Eucalyptus, including insights into the mating biology of the genus.
items.authors: N. Pham, BD Wingfield, S. Marincowitz, Y. M. Marpaung, Alinaswe P. Selebi, M. Tarigan
items.abstract: The Cryphonectriaceae (Diaporthales, Ascomycota) accommodates numerous important fungal pathogens that cause branch and stem canker diseases on woody plants worldwide. These include, for example, Cryphonectria (Cry.) parasitica, the causal agent of chestnut blight, which caused the near eradication of the American chestnut (Castanea dentata) in North America. The profound ecological and economic impact of Cry. parasitica has prompted considerable research interest in the diversity, biology, and pathogenicity of other species in the Cryphonectriaceae globally. During a 2023 disease survey in North Sumatra, trees of a single Eucalyptus clone dying as result of infection by the vascular wilt pathogen Ceratocystis (Cer.) manginecans were also found to have structures typical of the Cryphonectriaceae on their bark. The aim of this study was to identify this fungus, to test its pathogenicity and to consider its mating biology in comparison to other related species. DNA sequence comparisons for six loci (ITS, LSU, TUB1, TUB2, TEF1, and RPB2), phylogenomic analyses, as well as morphological observations, revealed that the fungus was an undescribed species of Cryphonectria, for which the name Cry. eucalypticola is provided. Inoculation trials on four eucalypt genotypes showed that Cry. eucalypticola is only mildly pathogenic and different eucalypt genotypes differed in their susceptibility to infection. Mating-type locus analysis based on whole-genome data showed that the fungus is homothallic. Analyses of the genomes of six other Cryphonectria species showed for the first time that, the genus includes both homothallic and heterothallic taxa. items.title: In a World Short on Big Discoveries, Offshore Oil Companies May Need To Double Down on Intervention Work
items.authors: Trent Jacobs
items.abstract: There’s an old cliché in the upstream business that may be increasingly worth repeating. “The best place to find oil is in an oil field,” attribution unknown. Among the industry groups that have always held this old chestnut close to heart is the subsea well intervention community. For decades, this niche business has fought to make its case to offshore oil companies that reinvesting just a fraction of the original capex spent on what are often multibillion-dollar assets is very much worth it. There is also a new and mounting pressure on oil companies to sustain production from existing offshore fields as it becomes increasingly difficult to find new ones big enough to justify major infrastructure investments. This message was made by several speakers to those attending the recent SPE Subsea Well Intervention Symposium in Galveston, Texas. Dave Wilson, vice president of investor relations at global energy services company Expro, said “the industry is being asked to produce more energy molecules with fewer people, less resources” and that well intervention offers a way to do so more efficiently. He noted that a decade’s worth of infrastructure is already in place, wells represent significant sunk costs, and relatively modest investments can generate large returns. Wilson said that when speaking with investors about the upstream sector, he compares new projects to planting a tree, while brownfield assets are like a mature tree with fruit still waiting to be harvested. items.title: Perilla essential oil-loaded gelatin-hyaluronic acid films for kiwiberry preservation: Effects of dual crosslinking on film properties and proteomic responses.
items.authors: Song Zhang, Qing-Rui Wang, Jian-Rui Hou, Hong-Yan Xu, Guang-Jun Xia
items.abstract: A dual-crosslinked gelatin-hyaluronic acid (HA) film loaded with perilla essential oil was developed for Actinidia arguta preservation. Ca2+ and gallic acid reinforced the film network, giving GH/Ca/A₃ high tensile strength (40.39 MPa), low water vapor permeability (3.34 g/m2·day), improved hydrophobicity, and enhanced thermal stability. During 12 days of storage, the essential oil-free gelatin-HA film (GH-K) reduced fruit weight loss from 40.01% to 17.98%, confirming its physical barrier-based preservation effect under ambient storage conditions. Perilla essential oil further enhanced preservation, reducing weight loss to 10.00%, maintaining firmness at 27.6 N, and lowering total colony and yeast/mold counts to 4.26 and 2.19 log CFU/g, respectively. Proteomics showed that GH/P-K modulated antioxidant defense, glutathione metabolism, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, redox regulation, and cell wall-related pathways, linking film performance with delayed kiwiberry deterioration.

items.title: Structural programmability of jujube polysaccharides: Extraction, molecular architecture, and microbiota-mediated fermentation Design for gut-Brain-Axis-Relevant Applications.
items.authors: Fengling Liu, Zhihui Luo, Sidra Jabeen, Gang Liu, Pan Li, Tao Wu
items.abstract: Jujube polysaccharides (JPs) are heterogeneous food pectic glycans, but how extraction and post-isolation modification define their molecular architecture and microbiota-accessible functionality remains insufficiently integrated. This review critically synthesizes evidence linking extraction conditions to JP structural templates and evaluates how post-isolation remodeling tunes molecular weight, RG-I/HG balance, side-chain architecture, esterification, charge, conformation, and assembly state. Using an evidence-stratified framework, we distinguish direct JP findings from mechanisms inferred from broader pectin and dietary-fiber literature. We propose that backbone architecture, RG-I-associated side chains, esterification, and supramolecular organization may shape microbial accessibility, fermentation kinetics, selective utilization, short-chain fatty acid production, and gastrointestinal substrate availability. This structure-microbiota-metabolite perspective supports a validation pipeline based on defined JP fractions, matched pectin controls, standardized fermentation models, and causal microbiome designs. Gut-brain-axis relevance is discussed as an indirect, evidence-limited downstream implication rather than an established JP mechanism.
